Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

issues.explanation: These trigger items are hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of physical abuse by a romantic partner. Fire/flames and snakes suggest trauma content not represented anywhere in the memory or appraisal items and not plausibly linked to partner physical abuse unless there were specific undisclosed trauma details. The rest of the profile centers on bodily pain, terror, injustice, contamination, and identity change following interpersonal assault, so these two triggers appear clinically incoherent with the formulation and with the other selected items.

issues.item: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: A snake-specific trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile for physical abuse by a romantic partner. The memory and appraisal items center on bodily pain, terror, contamination, and injustice related to interpersonal assault, but no other item suggests animal-related trauma content. This makes the snake trigger clinically incoherent with the trauma type and with the trigger-memory-appraisal pattern in the formulation.

vignette:
Kwame is a 30-year-old African American man who works as a curriculum designer for a public education nonprofit, a job that used to suit the parts of him he valued most: careful thinking, creativity, and a sense that he was helping build something useful for other people. He is single now, though when he first speaks about the relationship that brought him to treatment, he still catches himself referring to his former partner as if the relationship might somehow resume. The traumatic event he returns to most often happened late one evening in the apartment they shared. They had both been drinking, and he remembers the sharp smell of alcohol on his partner’s breath and clothes before he remembers the first blow. What began as an argument about his family escalated when his partner mocked him for “always choosing them” and made cutting comments about the kind of family he came from. Kwame remembers trying to end the conversation and move toward the kitchen, where something had begun to burn on the stove, filling the apartment with a bitter scorched smell. In the confusion of shouting, alcohol, and that burnt odor spreading through the room, his partner hit him repeatedly. When he recalls it now, the scene remains fused together in those sensory details: the taunting comments about family, the fumes of liquor, the smell of something burning, and the conviction in that moment that he was in real danger.

In the days and weeks after, Kwame found that the memory did not feel like something settled in the past. When it returned, he did not experience it as a distant recollection but as something that seemed to happen again inside his body. He describes feeling pain in the same places where he was struck, as if his ribs, shoulder, and face briefly remembered before his mind could put words to anything. What frightened him most was that the terror came back too. He could be sitting quietly at home or at his desk reviewing lesson materials, and suddenly the same jolt of fear would seize him, immediate and total, with no reassuring sense that the event was over. Sometimes, even when he was only thinking about that night, he could smell what he had smelled then: alcohol, and underneath it the acrid burnt scent from the kitchen. He found this especially disturbing because it made him question whether he could trust his own mind. He had come to believe that something about him had been altered so deeply that he was no longer recognizable to himself. The man he had taken himself to be—steady, thoughtful, composed—felt replaced by someone jumpy, ashamed, and preoccupied by things he could not control.

Certain moments in ordinary life became unexpectedly difficult. At work, colleagues often made casual conversation before meetings, and harmless remarks about family—holiday plans, whether he was visiting relatives, jokes about mothers calling too often—could cause him to go still and lose track of what was being discussed. He would keep his face neutral, but internally he was back in that apartment, hearing his partner weaponize family against him. Office social events became hard to tolerate if someone arrived smelling of beer or whiskey. He began leaving quickly, telling coworkers he had another deadline. Once, when a burnt smell drifted from the office kitchenette after someone left food too long in the toaster oven, he felt his body tense so suddenly that he had to step outside the building and stand on the sidewalk until he could steady himself. Over time he narrowed his routines to avoid these moments when he could. He ate lunch alone more often, skipped after-work gatherings, and avoided visiting friends if he thought there might be drinking.

Alongside this, Kwame carried a heavy sense of violation that he struggled to describe without sounding, to his own ears, melodramatic or weak. He kept returning to the thought that what happened to him was profoundly unfair and that nothing had been done about it. He did not feel there had been any real acknowledgment of the harm. That unresolved injustice sat with him every day. He also spoke, with visible discomfort, about feeling dirty because of what happened. He knew intellectually that being assaulted did not make him contaminated, but the feeling persisted anyway. After memories of the assault, he sometimes showered longer than he intended, scrubbing hard at his skin while knowing that what he wanted to wash off was not physical dirt.

By the time he sought help, these patterns had begun to cost him. He was still performing at work, but with increasing effort, and his isolation had become noticeable to people around him. He said he was tired of arranging his life around smells, comments, and sudden bodily jolts that made him feel as if he were no longer living in the present. What finally brought him in was a recent meeting at work in which a coworker made an offhand remark about “family drama,” and another came in carrying the smell of alcohol from a lunch event; Kwame felt the terror and physical pain rise so forcefully that he had to end the meeting early. He came to treatment afraid that this unrecognizable version of himself was permanent, and hoping, cautiously, that he might one day remember what happened without feeling his body and mind dragged back into it.
